what_its_for: This device delivers a quick dose of insulin called a 'bolus' to help control your blood sugar after meals or to correct a high blood sugar reading. It works alongside your continuous background (basal) insulin to keep your blood sugar levels in a healthy range throughout the day.
how_to_take: Your insulin pump delivers insulin through a small flexible tube (called a cannula) placed just under your skin, usually on your belly, thigh, upper arm, or buttocks. To give a bolus dose: (1) Check your current blood sugar level using your meter or continuous glucose monitor (CGM). (2) On your pump screen or connected device, enter the amount of carbohydrates you are about to eat, or enter your current blood sugar if you are correcting a high. (3) The pump will calculate a suggested dose — review it carefully. (4) Confirm and press the button to deliver the dose. (5) Eat your meal within 15 minutes of giving a meal bolus unless your doctor tells you otherwise. Always make sure your infusion site looks healthy and is not red, swollen, or painful before giving a bolus.
dosing: Your dose is personalized and set by your diabetes care team based on your insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio (how much insulin covers each gram of carbohydrates you eat) and your correction factor (how much one unit of insulin lowers your blood sugar). Do NOT change these settings on your own. A typical bolus may range from 1 to 20 or more units depending on your meal size and blood sugar, but your exact dose will be calculated by the pump using your personal settings. The maximum single bolus dose this pump can deliver is 200 units. Always confirm the dose on the screen before pressing deliver.
missed_dose: If you forgot to give a bolus before your meal and you have already eaten, check your blood sugar level. If your blood sugar is high, you may need a correction bolus — contact your diabetes care team or follow their sick-day or correction guidelines. Do NOT give a double dose to make up for a missed one without checking your blood sugar first. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or diabetes educator right away.
storage: Store your insulin cartridges or reservoirs according to the insulin manufacturer instructions. Most insulins used in pumps (such as rapid-acting insulin like Humalog, Novolog, or Apidra) should be stored in the refrigerator (36°F–46°F / 2°C–8°C) until you are ready to use them. Once loaded into the pump, insulin can be kept at room temperature (below 98.6°F / 37°C) for up to 48–72 hours depending on the insulin type — check the insulin label for specifics. Keep your pump and insulin away from direct sunlight, extreme heat, and freezing temperatures. Do not store insulin in a car glove compartment or near a heating vent. Change your infusion set and insulin reservoir every 2–3 days as instructed.
what_to_avoid: Avoid exposing your pump to strong magnetic fields, X-ray machines, MRI machines, or CT scanners — always tell medical staff you wear an insulin pump before any imaging procedure. Avoid rough contact sports or activities that could damage the pump without proper protection. Do not go into hot tubs, saunas, or very hot baths for extended periods, as heat can degrade your insulin. Avoid drinking excessive amounts of alcohol, as this can cause dangerously low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). Do not ignore pump alarms or error messages — address them right away. Avoid reusing infusion sets, as this can cause infections or poor insulin absorption.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or diabetes care team right away if: your blood sugar is consistently too high or too low; you notice signs of infection at your infusion site (redness, swelling, warmth, or pus); you experience nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, or difficulty breathing, which may be signs of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA); your pump is alarming with an error you cannot fix; you run out of insulin; you feel confused, very shaky, or faint; or if you are unsure whether your pump is working correctly. Call 911 or go to the emergency room immediately if you lose consciousness or cannot swallow.
when_it_works: Rapid-acting insulin used in bolus pumps (such as Humalog, Novolog, or Apidra) starts working within 10–15 minutes, reaches its peak effect in about 1–2 hours, and lasts for approximately 3–5 hours. This is why it is important to give your bolus dose just before eating. Your blood sugar should start coming down within 1–2 hours after a meal bolus. Results vary depending on the injection site, your activity level, and individual metabolism.
special_populations: Pregnancy: If you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, work closely with your diabetes care team — insulin needs change significantly during pregnancy and close monitoring is essential. Children and Teens: Dosing must be carefully adjusted for children; always work with a pediatric endocrinologist. Elderly Patients: Older adults may be more sensitive to insulin and at higher risk for low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) — frequent blood sugar monitoring is important. Kidney or Liver Disease: These conditions can affect how your body processes insulin and may lower your insulin requirements — inform your doctor of any kidney or liver problems. Illness: When you are sick, your blood sugar can become unpredictable — follow your healthcare provider's sick-day rules and check your blood sugar more frequently.
